utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, the technical booth, the interpreters; good morning to the Office of the Prosecution and Defence counsel. I cannot say good morning this morning to General Krstic, but I think we have a written authorisation to continue the proceedings without his presence. Is that correct, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, colleagues of the Prosecution. I have been informed that in the course of last week or, rather, on Friday, that the Registrar received -- that the Registrar sent out a request and General Krstic said that he was willing to allow the proceedings to proceed without his presence today, and of course as we know, the reasons for his absence are medical reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We haven't got a written declaration then, have we?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His written declaration does exist and is probably with the Registry Office of this Tribunal, with the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that Madam Registrar has her microphone switched on to take the floor and bring us up to date. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We already have a copy of this letter with us, and we also filed that document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Petrusic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence will continue its examination of the next witness. But before the witness enters court, the Defence would like to move into private session and will be giving its reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move into private session, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your education and training and that you are a university graduate, can you tell us what knowledge, that is to say, what skills and education that faculty provides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the name of the faculty speaks for itself. It is the Faculty for Political Science, the National Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, let me just say before we go ahead, I should like to ask you to speak more slowly to facilitate the work of the interpreters and to make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will try. As I said, I graduated from the Faculty of Political Science, the Total National Defence Department. The word itself, "Total National Defence," speaks about the concept and Doctrine of All People's Defence in the then Yugoslavia, because the sociopolitical system as a system was one which functioned with this concept of total national defence in the case of an aggression against the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. At the faculty I gained knowledge about the concept and doctrine of national defence, and the faculty is fairly similar to the kind of knowledge you gain at military academies. In addition to the professional, tactical, and strategical composition, at my faculty we tend to focus on ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue but slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In studying the concept of total national defence, we look at all segments of society, the civilian structures and the organisation of total national defence for the whole area of the former Yugoslavia. I received the title of Professor of Total National Defence and received the rank of lieutenant in the reserve formations, which implies serving one's military duty in case of an aggression against the former Yugoslavia. And I had my wartime assignment in my original unit, like everybody else, all the other citizens of the country we lived in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that during your education and training you became acquainted with the basic types of weapons used by the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I underwent infantry training in the Marshal Tito Centre of Military Schools in Sarajevo, and I was trained in tactical training and marksmanship on the training grounds of Sarajevo, to the third level. I got to know all the weapons, how they were used, and what they were intended for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you completed your education and schooling, you received your wartime assignment, you said, and you were sent to a certain unit. How did that function according to the rules and regulations of Territorial Defence that were effective in the former JNA? Could you tell us something about that? That's right, that's what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you completed your education, did you start work in your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was employed in the municipality of Sokolac, attached to the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence of Sokolac, and I worked there up until 1990. Later on, because of my family situation, I went back to my native village where I did some other work that had nothing to do with my professional training and rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you worked in the Territorial Defence, could you tell us specifically what your work was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in the staff, in the Operations Department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you stopped working in the Territorial Defence Department and when you went back home to your native village, you continued to have your wartime assignment, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The start of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, in the area you lived in, where did it find you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when the war broke out, I was in the village of Sokolovici, near Sokolac, and that was in 1992. I received a call-up for mobilisation and I reported to the first wartime unit, according to my wartime assignment. That was the Romanija detachment. Later on, on the 21st of May, the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade was established, and I worked in that formation until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after you received your wartime assignment or, rather, after you reported, the 2nd Romanija Brigade had not yet been established; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, those were the -- it was a fledgling organisation, its just being organised. But very quickly -- it was formed very quickly later on. The wartime unit in the region was formed very quickly after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, tell us, please, what your concrete task was and job was in the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade? What did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started working in the Department for Moral Guidance and Religious Affairs, and this department was set up to inform the people, officers and soldiers, of the situation in which the Serbian people found themselves. This type of information involved informing the populous of the -- of what was going on around them. We saw that the people were motivated for their wartime assignments, for carrying out their combat activities, and we saw to relations between the units, that general respect should prevail. We saw to the psychological and physical capabilities of the people and how information and propaganda launched by the enemy were affecting the populous as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did every unit, that is to say -- let me rephrase that question. Was your work at the level of the command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, or did your work involve lower levels, if I can use that term, the level of the brigades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was at the level of the brigade commands, and it went down the ladder, down the chain of command, within the frameworks of the brigade. I worked in the 1st Motorised Battalion of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade which was at the defence lines at Olovo and Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you performed those duties, as far as I was able to understand, until 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, up to 1995, up to March of that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now move on to the events that took place at the beginning of July 1995. Tell us, please, where you were at the time and whether you continued to do the same work you were doing prior to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did do the same work, but from the 1st Motorised Battalion, I returned to the command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade and I worked in the same Department for Moral Guidance, Information, and Religious Affairs. And sometime at the beginning of July, my unit received orders to take part in the Srebrenica operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you acquainted with the plan of that operation and its goals, the operation Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Commander informed us about that, and I think the main Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. goal was to execute the operation, that is, to narrow down the zone, the protected enclave of Srebrenica, and to cut off the corridor Srebrenica-Zepa. And the reason for that was that there were constant skirmishes of Muslims of the 28th Division which was located in Srebrenica, and their skirmishs in Serbian villages and the killing of the population and passing through the Srebrenica-Zepa corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you have broached that subject, you are talking about the attacks and skirmishes that took place although Srebrenica was in the other zone; that is to say, another brigade covered that area. But to quote an example, that kind of reporting, should it have been -- was that your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. Could you repeat that, please? What do you mean, reporting?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the job you were doing, your duties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that from the safe area there were skirmishes by the Muslim forces of the 28th Division, that is. So within the frameworks of your work --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I see, yes. It was up to the Information Service, Information Department, to inform the soldiers and their commanding officers realistically of what was going on around Srebrenica for them to gain a proper insight into what was actually going on, realistic information, because the information media put out quite different information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which information media do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim information media, those belonging to the Muslim forces. Those were the ones that we had access to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in listening to that information media and the information that you got, you were there to actually say the -- to tell the actual state of affairs, what actually existed, give a realistic view. Could you tell us when you started out on your assignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started on the 4th and 5th of July, 1995, and we arrived in the Zeleni Jadar area and we set up camp around the village of Jasenova, that region there. And that facility is to the south of the urban area of Srebrenica, urban conglomerate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your unit moved off from that region towards Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We started out. Nothing happened on the first two days. I think that combat activities actually started on the 6th and 7th, perhaps even the 8th of July. And my unit was assigned the task of taking up position at a feature called Alibegovac. That is a broader region, and it is called -- the region is called Alibegovac. We arrived at the Alibegovac position on the 10th of July, and that is where we stopped because we were ordered not to enter Srebrenica but just to narrow down the enclave, to make it easier to defend the surrounding Serbian villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that order that you have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Commander explained the order to us, and it said to secure this area from combat activities, and this means the morale of the soldiers as well, their psychological capacitation for that operation, and that was my duty. I had to explain to the soldiers and to their commanding officers what they were supposed to do, what their behaviour should be, to boost their morale, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of these combat operations, did you, in fact, comply with the order, act on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because -- that is to say, we had our direction of movement. There was no resistance from Muslim forces, so that we took control of that feature fairly easily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you captured that feature on the 10th of July, and you stated with some certainty that date as opposed to the beginning, when you were not quite sure whether it was the 6th or the 7th that the operation started. So tell us, why is it that you remember the 10th of July so well for you to be able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember it because on the 11th of July, we already entered the urban area of Srebrenica, which means that Srebrenica, in military terms, had been liberated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in the command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. Do you know who was in charge of the Operation Krivaja 95, as it was code-named?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Krivaja 95 was under the command of General Radislav Krstic, but the forward command post in Pribicevac, he was there and we received his commands until the 10th of July, when Alibegovac fell. However, as I was in the command, I was able to hear the orders issued by the Commander to the unit. Once we had captured this feature, Alibegovac, I can't remember whether I ever heard him on the line, but he did not issue us orders. We received direct orders from General Ratko Mladic from there on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you quite sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, excuse me for interrupting you. Perhaps the names should be stated clearly. The witness said that the Commander explained an order. Perhaps we should say who that Commander was. Then again she said the Commander of the unit spoke over the radio. Perhaps you should tell us the name. You know the names, we don't, so would you please give us the names. Mr. Petrusic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a general question: You are a member of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade. Who was the Commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Commander was Colonel Mirko Trivic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you are referring to the Commander, when you have been using the term "commander" so far, did that refer to Colonel Mirko Trivic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively I was referring to Colonel Mirko Trivic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean he was your Commander until the 10th of July, and he received orders until the 10th of July from General Krstic. So I'm just going over what you have already said. So from the 10th of July onwards, your Commander, Mirko Trivic, received his commands from General Ratko Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, are you sure that you heard that on the 10th of July, commands were issued to Mirko Trivic by General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it. I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that command issued over the so-called Motorola?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several types of communications equipment were used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the line, it was always General Ratko Mladic and Colonel Mirko Trivic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear Krstic on the lines issuing orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I do not recollect him issuing orders. There may have been a conversation but no concrete orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Srebrenica fell on the 11th of July. Your unit, the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, did it enter the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade did not enter the town because, as ordered, it remained at Bojna, the village of Bojna, to the left of Srebrenica. Only the command members entered the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who were the members of the command? Were you among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. There was the Brigade Commander, Colonel Trivic; then the logistics officer -- do I need to give his name? Captain Dalivoji Podrevic, the Communications Company Commander, Milan Stanic, several communications signalsmen, and the escort of the Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Commander of one of the battalions there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Also the Battalion Commander, Major Ljubomir Eric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these proceedings, Witness D/C -- let me rephrase that question for a moment. You passed through Slapovici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I passed through the refugee camp, as it was called in those days, several times. It was a settlement with 1.000, maybe up to 2.000 refabricated buildings. And every night when we returned to the village of Jasenova, where our camp was, we would pass through this village. And even on the 13th of July, as we were withdrawing, we passed through Slapovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have heard here that Slapovici was set on fire and shelled, so my question has to do with that. Was Slapovici burned down partially or totally, just a few buildings or the whole settlement? Can you tell us more about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, that is not true. Slapovici was not touched, not by a single soldier. On the 13th of July, in the morning, I went via Jasenova, Slapovici, Srebrenica, and until that day, it was intact. Troops just went past this settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, in the introductory part of your testimony, you said that you are acquainted with weapons and artillery pieces that the former JNA had at its disposal, as well as the army of Republika Srpska. In the course of these proceedings, we have heard that an exceptionally large number of shells was fired at the town of Srebrenica itself and its environs, and even on the column of refugees moving from Srebrenica towards Potocari. And since you said that you yourself were in the town of Srebrenica, tell us, please, whether the town of Srebrenica was damaged, and generally, during your stay in the area, did you hear or see artillery weapons being fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some fire from artillery weapons but very little. The fire was targeted at fortified Muslim positions. There was no need to do that. The town of Srebrenica was not shelled at all. Not a single shell fell on the urban part of town, not a single building was damaged when we entered the town on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have heard here that within a span of several hours, 200 shells were fired; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I said that there was some artillery fire but of very limited extent, and it was mostly targeted at Muslim bunkers. But there wasn't any real need because the resistance that they put up did not require artillery action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you entered Srebrenica on the 11th of July, did you find civilians or soldiers or the inhabitants of Srebrenica there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. They had already left, I think, to the region of Potocari village. On the street I saw two dead men who were probably killed by small arms' fire, and we also saw a woman whose throat had been slit. We didn't know who it was. Then her brother came and told us that it was a Serb woman who had stayed to live there during the war, and if it hadn't been for him, we wouldn't have known the identity of that woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your stay in that area, did you have any contact with soldiers or representatives of UNPROFOR who were protecting the safe area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One occasion we had contact with them. This was prior to the fall of the Alibegovac feature. That day we saw two APCs of the Dutch Battalion heading towards the Muslims, along a macadam road. The Muslims opened fire at them, and we saw that. And we saw that one soldier was wounded. Actually, we thought that he had been wounded, but later we learnt that he had been killed. Later on, I can't remember whether that was that day or the next day, two APCs started off in our direction. I really don't know how to describe this. In fact, they surrendered to my unit. There were two complete crews of six or eight soldiers and two commanders, and it was explained to them to abate their fears. First they were frightened but we managed to explain to them that they would be free and that they could go back to their own country. I don't know how they were transported out, whether it was with an escort or not. I don't know. But anyway, they were directed towards Bratunac via Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, nothing special. We had some beer. It was quite warm. I offered them beer. They were glad to drink it because for a long time they had been living in the enclave outside the urban area, so that beer was rare. They were quite young. We exchanged greetings. They may have been 18 or 20 years old. I didn't really pay any special attention to them. Nobody mistreated them, as far as I was able to see, and they were simply escorted out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they leave on their APCs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, but -- how else? The only thing I'm not sure about was whether they were escorted. Probably they were, because there were some other activities ongoing. There were reports we were working on, so I didn't have much time to pay attention to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You entered the town of Srebrenica on the 11th, in the afternoon, together with the commanding officers you have mentioned. Where did you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We entered Srebrenica in the afternoon. Then we went -- the members of the command returned to the Jasenova camp, and my unit stayed in the village of Bojna, the Bojna feature, close to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Jasenova is where your headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the headquarters and the camp, as we call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, where was your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, when Srebrenica had fallen militarily, the unit was to assemble in the region of Viogora close to the Suceska village. That day we were tasked to search the terrain at the same time. So we followed the macadam road going from Mount Jahorina and we were to assemble at Viogora. However, from Srebrenica to Jahorina, it is about 10 to 12 kilometres, and it is highly inaccessible, so we moved on foot. On the road we didn't come across anyone, refugees or anyone else. We just walked across that area, searching the terrain. This was completed late in the evening, and there was no time for the unit to assemble and line up in the Viogora region. So we returned to camp, and the next day in the morning, my unit, together with the others, was assembled and lined up in the Viogora region. I did not attend the line-up because the command of the brigade was assigned the task to take the unit to Zepa. At the time I didn't really know what the order was and what the assignment of the unit would be, nor what we would be doing up there. So that on the 13th of July, in the morning, together with the Commander, Colonel Trivic, and the Commander of the Communications Company, I headed towards Zepa, the Zepa area, where our task was to set up camp and to find an area that would be suitable for a communications centre. My unit went to the roundabout way, Srebrenica, Jahorina, Suceska, probably also because of the crowds on the Srebrenica-Bratunac road, which was crowded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let us go back to the 12th or, rather, the 11th and the 12th of July. So on the 11th of July you left Srebrenica, and on the 12th and the 13th of July, did you at all see General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw General Krstic only on the 11th of July when we arrived in town. General Ratko Mladic came, also General Zivanovic, and then a little after them, probably because he had difficulty walking, General Krstic came, and I didn't see him again until the 13th, in the Zepa area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you, Colonel Trivic, and you just said the signalsman, you headed from Jasenova on the 13th, towards Bratunac. You passed through Srebrenica, Potocari, to reach Bratunac. Tell us, what did you see in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the UNPROFOR compound there. We saw a large number of women, men, and children, troops, members of the Dutch Battalion in camouflage uniforms; also people wearing civilian police uniforms. There was a large crowd of people. I didn't recognise anyone, at least not any of the senior officers of the Drina Corps that I knew at the time. And it was hard to pass through in a vehicle. We went through very slowly and we continued on the road to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you were able to see, that is, men, women, and children, were they mixed together or were they separated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not separated. They were all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After arriving in Bratunac, where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After Bratunac, we headed towards the Zepa area. The Commander, Mirko Trivic, was picked up by a command passenger vehicle which was to take him there, and the Commander of the Communications Unit was told to take the vehicle and to take me as well. So we drove from Bratunac via Kravica, Konjevic Polje, Nova Kasaba, Milici, Vlasenica, and the Zepa area, specifically the area of Pod Plane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Along the road from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje, did you come across troops, the police, convoys? Describe to us this trip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Along the road I did see all that you have mentioned. We caught up with a convoy that was driving Muslim refugees. It was a convoy of buses and trucks. I think that it is in the broader area of the village of Kravica. From the hills Muslim soldiers were firing and going in the direction of the road that we were on, as well as the convoy. On the other side of the road, soldiers, policemen, I saw people wearing olive-grey uniforms, as well as blue camouflage uniforms, were resisting. We started to overtake the convoy, though it was difficult to do. It was quite a risky trip; our lives were in danger. As the buses were higher than our vehicle, I couldn't see inside, who the people inside were. But several trucks -- in several trucks I could see that there were men, women, and children inside, as the trucks were not covered by canvas, they were open. The Muslim soldiers split up. There were a lot of them and they were quite close to the road. And they were firing at the convoy and the soldiers who were resisting. However, our aim was to get through as quickly as we could, and we continued along our way to the village of Pod Plane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We hear now for the first time that in the broader area of Kravica, that there were Muslim troops from the hills that had split up into small groups and that were firing at soldiers along the road, the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. Are you quite sure that they were Muslim soldiers or, rather, that that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am quite sure of that because I was passing through and we were trying to get through as quickly as possible to save our lives. There were very many soldiers. One could see it quite easily from the car. They were maybe 300, 400 metres from the road, and the distance between each one of them was 50 to 100 metres, the soldiers that were shooting. Our soldiers were lying down in a trench along the road. The fighting was going on and the convoy was passing through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You passed through Nova Kasaba. In Nova Kasaba there is a football pitch. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Along the road, in Nova Kasaba, did you see Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. After that convoy, we didn't see any larger group of people, be they prisoners or soldiers or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please try and remember what time it could have been when you passed through Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was in the morning, maybe before noon, because we reached close to Zepa around 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you reached the Pod Plane area on the 13th, at about 2.00 p.m. And combat operations towards Zepa, did they start that same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not that day. That day the units assembled; they arrived in the evening. It was still visible; I can't remember what time it was. Anyway, on the 14th of July, the operations started. There was reconnaissance by subordinate units, deployment, and actual combat was beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stayed until the end of the combat operations around Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed on until the 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that period of time, were you able to listen to communications among Commanders, that is, between your Commander and his Superior Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did have occasion to hear because we did listen to those conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in command of the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Krstic was in command of the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He issued direct orders to your Commander, Colonel Trivic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, preparing for your testimony, you told me so my question is: What do you know about the fact that when Zepa fell some technical equipment was seized, which included some documentation of the Zepa Brigade and the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that. I think that this was found in a school or something. I can't remember. It was a computer, actually, and some diskettes. There were rumours about that. I don't know what happened with that material later on, who took it over, so I can't be more specific, except to say that I know that it was found, that it included complete documentation regarding both Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, among the command staff of your Superior Command, did you see any of them at Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would see General Krstic most often. I also saw General Ratko Mladic. I saw some other senior officers from the Main Staff, as it was called then. Do I need to enumerate the names?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. Tell us who you saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Colonel Beara, Tolimir, officers from the Drina Corps who were with General Krstic, Colonel Vicic. Maybe if I would think a little harder I would remember some more names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw Colonel Vicic with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him from before, because he was my Commander at the school in Sarajevo so that I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, tell us, during the time of the combat operations towards Zepa, do you know which position, by establishment, was held by General Krstic and the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Krstic was first the Commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, later he became Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, and he held that position until, I think, the 20th of July. On the 20th of July, 1995, when the Commander of the Corps hitherto, General Zivanovic, retired, and by decree of the President of the Republic, he became the Commander of the Drina Corps. So this occurred around the 20th. We were informed around the 20th, while the Zepa operation was still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So around the 20th you were informed that General Krstic had taken over command over the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, from 1992 you were with General Krstic, I could put it that way, because he was your Commander of the brigade; then later on in July 1995, you were with him again in the Zepa and Srebrenica operations, so I assume that you know General Krstic well. So I would like to ask you whether you can tell us something about him as a Commander, as a personality, though in the army it is difficult to separate the two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can say quite a lot about General Krstic as a person, but primarily as a Commanding Officer. General Krstic was my Brigade Commander for some time, and later on, when he became Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, we frequently had contact with him because my unit, the 2nd Romanija Brigade, was part of the Drina Corps. When he took up duty as Brigade Commander, General Krstic was Lieutenant Colonel. He formed and organised the 2nd Romanija Brigade in such a way that I think it could not compare -- there was no other unit that could compare with it because everything functioned perfectly in the unit, though it was quite a large unit by establishment. We all came to know him and to love him, I must say, primarily because of his character, his behaviour as a military man, the way he treated his subordinates, the civilian population, his superiors, captured Muslims and Croats. All that we were able to see and hear about him and our experience working with him has suddenly been totally undermined, and I simply cannot understand why he should have been accused. Because later when we learnt what had happened in the environs of Srebrenica, he could not have ordered that to happen, because throughout the war, everything he did and said was quite in the opposite sense. We did have Muslim prisoners who were held in the Knezina detention centre for some time, that is where the brigade command was, and they were treated as any other people. They had coffee, they had cigarettes; they were maybe better off than Serb soldiers sometimes. In due time they were exchanged. And even now we have contacts with some of them in Sarajevo and they are grateful for the way they were treated by us. In 1993 General Krstic helped the Croats and troops of Vares. He helped the troops and people of Vares, with all their equipment, to reach Sokolac, to save them from the Muslim attacks. And a kind of refugee camp was set up there and they stayed there, some 15 days, some a whole month, and then they went on from there as they wished. The military and the equipment crossed over to territory under the control of the Croatian army. I don't know exactly where. In those days, many inhabitants of Sokolac, which was within the area of responsibility of General Krstic's units, were opposed to him. They did not approve. They were saying, "Why did he as a Commander of a Serb unit, why was he saving the Croatian people?" As for captured people, I never heard him say that a prisoner should be mistreated or anything like that. He always protected them. And I liked his attitude as a professional military man. He treated people with respect. He fully observed the rules of war, and he was very well-versed in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, I will stop there. I have no more questions for you. It will now be the turn of my learned friends from the Prosecution to continue to put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. I'm looking at the clock, and from the point of view of organisation, perhaps it would be a good idea to have a break. But with respect to the day's schedule as a whole, this could complicate matters for us. But I think that we could have a rest. Let's take a break, a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's going to be Mr. Harmon who is going to start the cross-examination. Yesterday we spoke about Article 90, (G) and (H), and as the examination-in-chief took more or less an hour, with flexibility with which we take the Rule, please keep that in mind, members of the Prosecution. Witness D/C, have you had a rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are now going to be answering questions put to you by the Prosecution, Witness D/C.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my colleagues from the Defence. Cross-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness D/C.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we can go into private session for the first set of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us move into private session. I suppose this has to do with matters of identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, you described in your direct examination the concrete tasks that you had in the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade. You identified one of those tasks as a responsibility to inform the officers and the soldiers about the situation in which the Serb people found themselves. Can you explain that a little bit more, please, what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That means to inform the soldiers and officers with the prevailing circumstances, to inform them of their environment, both immediate environment and the broader environment; the state of affairs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the territory where the unit is located, the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the state of affairs in the other republics of the former Yugoslavia, and the situation and relationship of the International Community towards the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. This also included the relationship of the Muslim people towards the Serbian people and vice versa; the territory in which they live, where they belong, what the object of the fight of the Serbian people was, the objective of defence, things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where would you get your information about the view that the International Community had vis-a-vis the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got official information from the Superior Commands, and this went down the chain of command, and also via the information media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you get information about negotiations that were ongoing between the Serbs, the Muslims, and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We received that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive information about United Nations' developments, such as the views and Resolutions of the United Nations vis-a-vis, for example, the attack on the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We received that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive information from -- let me ask you -- let me withdraw that question. When was it that you received that information in relation to the attack on the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear what you're asking me, whether when we moved towards the enclave or the events around the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me clarify my question. When was it that you received information about developments at the United Nations and their view, their Resolutions, that related to Srebrenica? In July of 1995, in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, information about the position taken by the United Nations towards the safe area, we got that earlier on. But the Muslims did not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. respect the Resolution, and because of all the armed attacks on the Serbian population --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. If you just answer the question that I ask you, I'm going to try to be fairly precise in my questions. Were you aware that the United Nations, following the attack on Srebrenica, was concerned about the fate of thousands of Muslim civilians and prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the fall of Srebrenica, well, at that time we didn't really because we continued towards the Zepa operation, so we had no separate information as to the position of the United Nations, just concrete information. And via the public media we learnt what we could from them. We heard different information from the Federation; that is to say, the Muslims conveyed, carried, different information which did not correspond to the actual situation that we found on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you heard Muslim information through the radio, I take it, and through the television and other media sources that there were thousands of Muslim men --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- who were massacred following the fall of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were an officer in the VRS at the time dealing with the issue of informing the soldiers and the officers about the situation in which they found themselves; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform your soldiers and your officers about the reports that you had heard on the Muslim media that thousands of Muslim civilians and prisoners of war had allegedly disappeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did inform them. But those reports, the reports coming in, and the casualties around Srebrenica, we learnt about that much later on; two to three months, perhaps, after the fall of Srebrenica. The first information came over the media much later, and immediately after the fall of Srebrenica, we knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear on the 17th of July that the spokesperson for President Karadzic issued a public statement in which he alleged or said that there were very serious allegations about the Muslim civilians and prisoners of war who had gone missing but that he personally did not give that any credit? Did you hear about that statement issued by Mr. Zametica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At that time I did not hear about that, only later on, because we were already engaged in combat activities again and we had no occasion to listen to the information media and hear information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So in performing your duties while you were in Srebrenica and in Zepa, were you in an information blackout? You didn't get any information about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't an information blockade or blackout. The circumstances were as they were. But most of the work I did at the time focused on information and what the tasks of the units were; to take care of the people on the terrain, to solve the problems that cropped up, the problems that they were facing daily, whether they had psychological problems or anything of that kind, perhaps medical problems, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at least that aspect of your job you were unable to fulfil because you didn't have information at your disposal; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not that I couldn't fulfil it. But according to the existing structure and hierarchy that existed in the army at that time, there was no need for that information. We didn't know about the events that had taken place, the occurrences. We were not informed about the occurrences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll return to that topic in a few minutes. But let me now concentrate on your role in the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade. You testified that you received orders to go to Srebrenica sometime before the attack commenced on the enclave, and you testified that you at some point in time reached the Alibegovac feature on the 10th of July. Now, up to that point in time, your unit had not had any resistance, had they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Smaller resistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, your unit didn't suffer any casualties up through the 10th of July, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your testimony -- let me see if I understand the structure of your unit. The 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, the Commander was Lieutenant Colonel Mirko Trivic; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Mirko Trivic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did he have a deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did have a deputy, but in the Srebrenica operation he wasn't there. He remained in his original unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was his second in command in the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Srebrenica operation he did not have a deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was solely in charge of commanding the units under him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your role in that operation, can you explain to us exactly what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Primarily, pursuant to orders, I had to explain to the soldiers and the commanding officers, the subordinate Commanders, what the object of our operation was for them to be able to understand why they were there, why they had come there, what their goal was; and to follow and monitor their work, to write reports, to do reporting for the command, to observe their physical and psychological stability and the ability to stand up to the situation, the effects that enemy propaganda was having on them, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it those responsibilities took you into the field, away from Colonel Trivic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Sometimes I was there; sometimes I was touring the soldiers in the units, going from one to another. But it was a small unit so we were mostly all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you with Colonel Trivic at all times during the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Twenty-four hours a day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a communications centre associated with your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was located in the village of Jasenova, and we had communications on the terrain as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the communications centre -- the principal communications centre for your unit was not the location Alibegovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was one there. The communications centre was set up at Jasenova, but all the devices that functioned in Jasenova functioned at Alibegovac as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what type of devices did you use at Alibegovac? Did you use hand-held Motorolas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Motorolas and hand-held receivers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this question, Witness D/C: Who would be in a better position to know what orders, if any, were given by General Mladic, you or Colonel Trivic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was present there and I could have heard. It's almost the same thing. He would receive the orders and I just listened to them, I heard them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you ever receive any orders from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me return to my question again. During the operation involving your unit, who was in the better position to know what orders were received from General Mladic, if any, you or Colonel Trivic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Trivic, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read you a statement from Colonel Trivic. Colonel Trivic was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has an objection to the reading of that statement. The statement was not provided in the court. The Defence does not have that statement, it has not had an opportunity to get to know it, so I do not think that this statement should be read to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I take a contrary view to that. This statement was provided to us on the 5th of October by Colonel Trivic, who was interviewed, pursuant to a summons. This witness has testified about certain facts. I'm going to read her the views of Colonel Trivic in respect of certain parts of her testimony and ask her to comment on it, and I think that is a fair and appropriate way to examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Are you going to make the statement available to the Defence so they can see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This statement, if they want to see it, I will make it available but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consider that statement -- that that statement should have been provided to the Defence earlier because of the examination-in-chief. And in this case, we are going to be handicapped, in a handicapped position, because we're going to get the statement now in the course of this testimony, and what do we do with it now at this late date? The Prosecutor knew seven to ten days beforehand that this witness would come to court, and he knew the contents of this witness' testimony. I, therefore, consider that he was duty-bound to provide the Defence with the statement if he had the intention of referring to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I comment on that? May I comment on my colleague's remarks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for us to be able to make a decision in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the first place, we received a very brief and scant summary, mostly topical, about this witness' testimony. The Prosecutor complained about that on two occasions. So to assert that the Prosecutor knew what this witness was going to say is simply not correct. Second of all, if this transcript is to be made available to the Defence, I would ask that, 1, it be kept -- it be returned to us, it not be disseminated. This is a statement that was provided to us pursuant to orders of the Prosecutor. It is a statement that relates to the investigation, and, very frankly, Mr. President, I would prefer making available to the witness the aspects of the statement about which I'm going to examine and not all aspects of this, because other parts of this are sensitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to consider the matter, and this will take a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has decided that the Prosecutor may use, to test the credibility of the witness, this statement. The Defence can have the right to re-examination after having inspected the document. That is the decision of the Chamber; that is to say, the Prosecutor will be duty-bound to provide the document to the Defence for the Defence to be able to study the document and then have the right to re-examine the witness with respect to that question. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just add, only the parts of the document which are relevant, because you said that other parts are supposed to be kept for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read to you what Colonel Trivic told us in respect of the very point on which you testified. Questioned by Mr. Ruez: [as read] "Q. Did you have direct communication with General Mladic from forward command post, or did the communication go through other people?" I'm sorry. Let me read from a few lines above that so I can get the totality of this. "Q. Was this the first time that you were aware General Mladic was in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew before we were in contact through radiolink because he contacted us from the forward command post of Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about Pribicevac command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, probably. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since -- do you remember what day did General Mladic in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have direct communication with General Mladic from forward command post or did the communication go through other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the signal officers, communication officers or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the topic of the communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some warning that we will encounter some air raids, air strikes, just to secure -- just to -- I don't know who conveyed that information to him. But since he was the only -- since he was the one who directly conveyed that information to us, just to secure the manpower, actually to find the proper shelter for them, because the air strikes were expected. I know that at the certain moment that the communications soldier was surprised first to hear Mladic on the radio, and then, second, he said, 'Fuck it. We are expecting the air raids. We have to find shelter.'

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any other orders coming directly from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what sense? About the engagement of the unit or what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whatever. Whatever. There were direct instructions coming from his mouth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not until the moment I greeted him, and when I was asked to secure the west part, but that was in close contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. At the moment he gave you that order, was he in the presence of Zivanovic and General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were together. Yes, I got close to him and I saluted him as my superior officer, and then I was tasked to secure that on an order to prevent possible attacks and surprises. I think that at that moment he addressed to all present commanding officers, saying that we should be ready for further movement toward Potocari." That conversation took, all in all, around ten minutes. So I've read you -- I've finished reading the statement that was made by Colonel Trivic to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 5th of October, and according to Colonel Trivic, who you say was in a better position to know the orders, Colonel Trivic informed us that the only order that he received from General Mladic was when he greeted Mladic in town at a ten-minute union. Do you care to comment on Colonel Trivic's statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can comment. That statement refers to the day of the 11th, when we entered Srebrenica, which means that previous orders were not reproduced there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll move on with your testimony. Now, let's talk about the meeting that you had in Srebrenica with General Mladic, General Zivanovic, and General Krstic. That meeting lasted about ten minutes, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't a real meeting, it was just an encounter in the street. But I was speaking about the orders prior to Alibegovac, prior to the 10th of July, that we received from Pribicevac, and the orders once we received Alibegovac on the 10th, the orders on the 11th, while we were entering Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot deny that General Mladic directly commanded the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General Mladic was the Chief of the Main Staff, and his subordinate officer was General Krstic, who was at that time the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Krstic was directly subordinate to the Commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic, and also one can say that he was subordinate to the Commander of the Main Staff, as was the whole Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Krstic issue any orders to the Drina Corps and to members of the attacking units after the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that. I didn't hear them on the communication lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Mladic order the -- I'm sorry. Did General Krstic order the units to proceed to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Mladic gave orders to the Brigade Commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let us talk about the orders that were given to the Brigade Commanders. Were you present when those orders were given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's just follow the sequence and the correct time order. After you had this brief ten-minute meeting with General -- where you saw General Mladic and the other officers in Srebrenica, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The command staff of my unit returned to the camp in Jasenova, and the unit itself stayed at the village of Bojna, close to Srebrenica, actually securing the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night between the 11th of July and the morning of the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent the night at the camp in Jasenova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you with Colonel Trivic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened briefly on the -- strike that. I'll withdraw that question. Were you present when Colonel Trivic was ordered to attend the meeting at a television repeater approximately 800 metres south of Srebrenica? This is on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was present when he received that order, and I was present when he left. But I was not present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that at that meeting that took place between your commanding officer and General Krstic and Colonel Obrad Vicic, that General Krstic issued an order to sweep the terrain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know who issued the order to sweep the terrain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following that meeting that took place at about 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning, did Colonel Trivic return, and did he tell you that he had received an order from General Krstic to sweep the terrain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he returned and he told us that he had received an order but not from Krstic. I think that Krstic was not there, already there. Anyway, he didn't tell us who he received the order from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your unit, in fact, sweep the terrain after the return of Colonel Trivic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We went from Srebrenica, towards Jahorina. It is about 10 or 20 kilometres away. We moved on foot. We went parallel with the road going from Srebrenica to Jahorina, and then from there on, Viogora and Suceska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read you what took place at that meeting and ask you to comment on what Colonel Trivic says occurred at that meeting at 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning of the 12th. "Q. We are now --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic. Is there a problem in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the objection, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already said that she was not present at the meeting. The Prosecutor is now going to read an extract from a statement by a person who attended that meeting. I cannot assume what the Prosecutor wants from the witness. But I do wish to draw attention to the fact that if the Prosecutor determines what is relevant from that statement which needs to be shown to the Defence, in the opinion of the Defence, that is purely his own opinion. In our opinion, it would be preferable for the Defence to receive the whole statement of Colonel Trivic, especially since the Defence has already spoken to Colonel Trivic and he is on our list of witnesses, and also in view of certain discrepancies between the statement Colonel Trivic gave to the Prosecutor and what he told us. And I think that the relevance of parts of this statement is not up to the Prosecutor alone to determine, so I wish to object to this question. I am also addressing myself to the Trial Chamber regarding its prior decision: Could you please specify the concept of relevance on the basis of which the Prosecutor is selecting excerpts to disclose to the Defence? It is our submission that we need to be shown the whole statement so as to be able to judge for ourselves what is relevant and what is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Harmon, briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I am going to read what Colonel Trivic says and identify another officer who was present at that meeting and ask this witness to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm having trouble just making that linkage. Maybe you could be a little bit more specific about why you would be asking this witness to comment on a meeting at which she has declared she wasn't present? I mean, what kind of linkage would you hope to show later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, let me explain that, Judge Wald. This witness has said, 1, she was very close to Colonel Trivic; she was with him at all times; she was on his command staff. Presumably she's in a position to know from Colonel Trivic what orders Colonel Trivic received and what actions were taken as a result of those orders. This witness has testified today, just now, that she was aware that Colonel Trivic went to a meeting, that there was -- although she didn't know who was there -- I haven't identified all of the people who were there; that Colonel Trivic returned and that her unit conducted a sweep operation on the 12th. So this is to test this witness' credibility when she has informed this Chamber about certain facts on her direct examination. Presumably she's in a position to know, and if she doesn't, then she can answer that she doesn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have already decided that you may use this statement to check the credibility of the witness. As for divergencies that may exist between the statement given to the Prosecution and the Defence, we will see that in the examination-in-chief of the Defence and the cross-examination of the Prosecution. So these questions are now being put to check the credibility of the witness, and it is the Prosecutor that has certain doubts regarding the credibility, so it is up to the Prosecutor to determine which parts of the statement they will use. As for the re-examination of the Defence, it is these parts of the statement that will have to be used. So we uphold our decision, having given that explanation. Please continue, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a Drina Corps officer by the name of Obrad Vicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have known him for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the Srebrenica operation and during the Zepa operation, he was the operations officer for General Krstic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not a communications officer. He worked in the Drina Corps, in the Operations Department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a poor translation. I said operations officer, not communications officer. He was the operations officer for General Krstic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not for General Krstic but for the Drina Corps, and he was directly subordinated to General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we'll pass on this particular point and we'll move to another point, Witness D/C. After you conducted -- I'm sorry. After Colonel Trivic returned to the area after the meeting in the morning, your unit conducted a sweep operation. My question is: Did Colonel Trivic and did you participate in that sweep operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Colonel Trivic receive an order to report to a specific location while he was conducting that sweep operation? Did he leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The search was to have been done earlier because that same day, the unit was supposed to line up to move on. However, the search took longer because of the inaccessibility of the terrain, and in the evening, at the invitation of General Mladic, Colonel Trivic went to a meeting. That is what we were told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that invitation, did Colonel Trivic leave the sweep operation at or around 1800 or 1900 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, around 1800 or 1900 hours. That was the end of the operation, the end of our assignment. He didn't leave us in the course of the operation but once the task had been accomplished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he went to meet General Krstic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The communications conveyed that General Mladic was calling the commanding officers to a meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read you what Colonel Trivic has to say about this particular topic. This is Colonel Trivic. "A. So sometime, because we were moving slowly, cautiously along the road ..." Let me interrupt here for a second. That's the road that you testified about moving up with your unit. "A. ... and once we -- so sometime around 1800 or 1900 hours. It was summertime so the sun was still up. Actually, I was ordered to refer to the village of Viogor, and I was told that the commander of the operation, that's Krstic, is waiting for me there. I got to him and he was accompanied by Andric. He asked me to brief him about the situation, whether I was engaged in any kind of combat or something like that, but there was no fighting activities so I was tasked, he told me to stay at those positions. So I organised the outpost to organise the line and everything else and to get connected with adjacent units, and I think that was the time when he ordered me to refer to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters at 10.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uh-huh. So 12 July, 10.00 p.m., the request to go to the Bratunac headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I issued orders to my subordinates, I went back to the village, to the command post where I was before to pick up maps and some materials, and I made my way to Bratunac." Now, can you comment on what Colonel Trivic says when he says that he met with General Krstic and General Krstic ordered him to go to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters? Can you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that because Colonel Trivic did not inform us about all those details. We just heard over the communication lines, conveyed by the signalsman, that all the unit Commanders were being invited by the command of the Main Staff to the headquarters in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you have any reason to dispute what Colonel Trivic told the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not disputing those details because I'm not familiar with the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has already said that she cannot confirm these things. I don't understand this additional question if the witness has already clearly said that she cannot confirm or deny. I think that is the only logical conclusion from the witness' response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Harmon, please proceed. The witness has already answered, and may I remind you that you have a time limit. And if you're going to use that time, it's up to you how you're going to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you did not attend that meeting, did you, at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that at that meeting, General Mladic issued an order to General Krstic for General Krstic to issue an order to his subordinate units to move to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that General Mladic issued orders. All the unit Commanders were present and they received direct orders that the next day, in the morning, we were to move on Zepa. I have no other concrete information about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did General Krstic then issue orders to the subordinate units that they had to move to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Trivic, when he returned from the meeting, he immediately informed us what our next assignment was. And on the 13th, in the morning, we headed towards Zepa. I took a road via Srebrenica, Potocari, Bratunac, whereas my unit took the direction Srebrenica, Jahorina, Viogora, Suceska. I think that at Viogora --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about that in a few minutes. My question was: Are you aware -- I'm sorry. Did General Krstic then issue orders to your unit and other units that they should proceed to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not there. This was at Viogora. The units assembled there on the 13th, in the morning, and they were addressed by General Mladic, as far as I know. I cannot say whether Krstic was there. But when they reached Zepa, they said that they were directly addressed by General Mladic. Which other officers were present, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So as I understood your testimony, you were present with Colonel Trivic on the 13th at Viogora; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you leave --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Viogora on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 13th I wasn't at Viogora at all. Colonel Trivic, myself, and the Commander of the Communications Company took the direct road via Slapovici-Srebrenica-Potocari-Bratunac, whereas my unit and the other officers in command took the route Srebrenica-Viogora. And at Viogora they were lined up and addressed by General Mladic. So I wasn't present at all. I didn't take that route on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. My question was: Where was Colonel Trivic on the morning of the 13th? Was he at Viogora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
