utterances.text: Let me read to you now what Colonel Trivic has to say about the meeting of the 13th, in the morning, at Viogora. "Q. Okay. Fine. So we are, indeed, now the 13th of July, in the morning, and you are south of Srebrenica where your forward command post was initially located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is where I slept. In the morning I went to Viogora, somewhere here, to meet Mladic and Krstic, because they were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. supposed to address to the soldiers, speak to the soldiers." Now, further down, Mr. Ruez says: "Q. So we are now in this location where General Krstic and General Mladic are supposed to address the troops.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Who was the one speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave my report and Mladic addressed the soldiers. He explained to him about the new task, about the need to continue, that we cannot return to our base unit, base location. The way that he addressed to them is like every commander when he wants to boost the morale and ask the soldiers that they cannot go and take a bath and change their uniforms and do anything. In that kind of way, he was addressing the soldiers. So 'Is that clear?' Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's not what I said. When he left then, I had problems to calm down the situation. He has a big authority and we, who were supposed to execute the task, we had problems to organise, and those who were really in critical conditions to send them back in the base and bring the new forces to cover them up and stuff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Zivanovic was not present at the meeting, or was he?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. "A. No, no, no, I think he wasn't there. Only those two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have an idea, approximately, what hour it was when the two Generals were addressing the troops?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, the interpreters are asking you to slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I thought I did, but I'll slow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a conflict of interest. The interpreters want you to speak slowly and you wish to speak quickly because you can bring in more material. I don't know whether the witness can memorise all that and then answer your question, but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will slow down. I will pick up where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat: Colonel Trivic was asked the question by

utterances.speaker: MR. RUEZ
utterances.text: "Q. Do you have an idea, approximately, what hour it was when the two Generals were addressing the troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ten, eleven, in the late morning. I was given the route which I'm going to take with my troops. That's from there through Derventa, Milici, Vlasenica, Han Pijesak, and then to Krivaca." Now, your testimony this morning was that you were -- you first of all went with Colonel Trivic to Zepa. Colonel Trivic says he took a different route. Can you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can comment on that. I think that all the statements given by Colonel Trivic about the meeting refers to the meeting in Bratunac of the 12th. Whether he consciously or unintentionally confused the dates. But I state with full responsibility that on the 13th, in the morning, when the unit was formed in Jasenova, that very same moment we took a jeep, together with the Company Commander of Communications, we took the route Srebrenica, Bratunac, and from there to Zepa, and that Colonel Trivic could not have been at Viogora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And as for General Krstic, we found him at Zepa. So I don't understand that statement myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when Colonel Trivic says that he was present in Viogora at 10.00 or 11.00, in the late morning, and you testified that in the morning of the 13th, before noon, you were in Nova Kasaba, there's a radical difference, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's talk about your trip down the Bratunac-Milici road. When you went along that road, your testimony was that there were Muslim soldiers who were firing at the VRS soldiers and police who were alongside that road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you observe that fire fight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was happening -- I think this was near to the village of Kravica because there were quite a number of burned-down houses around; maybe in terms of kilometres, for 2 kilometres, roughly. I cannot tell you exactly. But this was quite a long stretch of road. Because the configuration of the ground was such that there was a hillside, and as you drove along the road you were able to see these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers from the Bratunac Brigade either injured or killed as a result of the fire fight that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. All the soldiers and policemen were lying down in the trench along the road, on the other side of the road, so I couldn't recognise them. I could only recognise their uniforms, the olive-grey and the camouflage blue uniforms worn by the civilian police. They were all lying down. I didn't really have time to pay attention to all that. We were trying to overtake the convoy to save ourselves, so we didn't have much time to look carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to present an exhibit as Prosecutor's Exhibit 791. It is for your consideration; I don't ask the witness to comment on this exhibit. And if it could be distributed to counsel as well. This exhibit, for the record, is a document that was seized by the Office of the Prosecutor from the Bratunac Brigade, and it is a list of soldiers from the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade who were killed between the 18th of April, 1992 and the 25th of September, 1995. And there are no casualties described in this for any of the days during which time the Srebrenica enclave was taken, and particularly the date of the 13th of July, which the witness has testified about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness D/C, we're going to play a film, and before we play this film, I'd like to ask you: When you were going along that road, did you see any anti-aircraft guns that were firing at the civilians who were in the hills?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I have a Prosecutor's exhibit, please, which is 766.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can watch the monitor, Witness, I'm going to ask you some questions about this. This is a film from the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The film continues; there's more to it than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this film was taken on the 13th of July, on the very same road that you went in your direction towards Zepa. Did you see those anti-aircraft guns firing into the hills?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The guns here are on the road all the time that I moved. There was a convoy of Muslims, buses/trucks, on that road, and we overtook them towards Konjevic Polje. It was an enormous column. And just soldiers with infantry pieces were lying down. Muslims also had infantry weapons. And this wasn't the situation on that road. Had it been so, we wouldn't have been able to pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And everybody seems to be shown to be on the road here in this clip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this is a film that was taken on the 13th of July by a Serbian journalist, and you can see that it is timed, dated, and referenced. So let me turn to the next clip, please, in just a minute. The Trial Chamber has heard testimony, Witness D/C, of a significant number of Muslim civilians coming down from the hills and surrendering to the VRS army units and police units that were alongside the road. I'm going to play you a film and I'm going to ask you to comment on it. I'll play two pieces of film. This is also taken on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And do we have the next clip, which is clip number 4?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the person in the blue helmet in this film? I want you to focus on that. Now, this is also a film from the 13th, Witness D/C, and according to the soldiers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is also a film from the 13th of July, and according to the soldiers who were interviewed by the journalist, Muslim civilians were surrendering all day. Did you see any of those surrenders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see that. I just remembered when they fired because the journey was dangerous and we had to keep taking over the column of buses and trucks. The column was an extremely long one. Later on I saw some soldiers lying down, but I didn't see any Muslim civilians there. Probably those who were shooting, who had rifles. We can see some dark figures. Whether they were wearing uniforms or civilian clothing, was not actually discernible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, do you have any translation of the dialogue which was happening between the people shooting?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This last clip?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, this last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I thought that had been distributed. It is Prosecutor's Exhibit 102A. It had been previously distributed. I thought there was a package that was available to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you see the Bosnian Serb soldier wearing a stolen UN blue helmet in this film?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw he had something blue on his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any Bosnian Serb soldiers along the Bratunac-Milici road wearing United Nations' gear that had been stolen, such as helmets, flak jackets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I couldn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any Bosnian Serb soldiers with megaphones calling up into the hills, urging the people to surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we have the last clip, please, number 5. And while we're showing this clip, Madam Registrar, if I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/1 and 7/2 prepared and available.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] How long have you been there? We were there two days and two nights, completely surrounded. What were your rifles? I didn't have a rifle. I'm a civilian. Civilian, all right, then have no fear. Were you very afraid? Who wouldn't be afraid. Go ahead. What the fuck. You're scared. Come on, have no fear. Hey, you journalist, how come he already arrived before they did? Hey, take off Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that shirt. This one? Yes. How did you get it anyway? Take it off. Fuck it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, that was a scene that was filmed near a location Sandici meadows that you passed by on the 13th of July. Did you see any civilians that were in the custody of the VRS soldiers or the police on the road as you drove through?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic. I apologise for interrupting, Witness. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence would like to ask the Prosecution, if possible, for precision purposes, of the answer that the witness is to give now, whether the Prosecutor can be concrete and tell us what time of day this film was made, this clip was made, and the concrete situation, because the witness said that she passed at a certain time of day, that she passed by that way at a certain time of day. Now, can the Prosecutor be more precise as to the time when this clip was taken? We know it was the 13th of July. But if the witness says that on the road to Bratunac-Konjevic Polje she passed at a certain time of day, we should like to ask the Prosecutor to be more precise as to the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, there is testimony from civilians that they surrendered all day long. The answer to my colleague is it's indicated on the film itself the time of this film. The time of the film of the anti-aircraft guns being fired into the hills is at 4.48; the time of the surrender is, again, also indicated, I believe that's at 4.12 in the afternoon. But the testimony that has been presented to the Trial Chamber is that there were surrenders all day long on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Harmon, but you could ask the witness what time she passed and then we can discuss that afterwards. But we must bear in mind the time as well, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. She testified on her direct examination that she travelled down that road sometime before noon. That's why I didn't ask her that question. But I would like to show the witness a series of exhibits. If they are prepared, first of all, I'd like to show Exhibit 8/1, if that could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is a location that you passed. It's called -- it's a warehouse in Kravica. It's an aerial view. And first of all -- and there are two buses located at this location. The Trial Chamber has heard testimony of a significant number of prisoners who were detained at this warehouse on the 13th of July and who were murdered at this location on the 13th of July. Did you pass this warehouse on the 13th of July, and did you see a large number of prisoners who were detained at that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember the warehouse because I don't know the area very well. I recognise the communication here. But when I was moving along the road, there were lots of buses and trucks transporting the Muslim people. That's not on the photograph. And at that time there were no -- there was nobody by the side of the road or any objects. I just saw that the Muslims were firing over a clear space, and we hurried up to pass that way as quickly as possible for our safety. I don't know that this is a warehouse at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you the next exhibit. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 7/4. This is the location of the film clip where you saw Muslim civilians surrendering. This is Sandici meadow. In this picture you will see a number of buses and you'll see a large grey mass in the middle, and there has been testimony that this constitutes many hundreds of civilians who were detained on this meadow. My question, first of all, is: You passed this meadow on the way to Zepa. Did you see a meadow where hundreds of civilians and prisoners of war were detained? Do you remember seeing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just in Potocari. I saw lots of civilians only in Potocari, men, women, children, and from that time on, buses arriving and trucks arriving. But on this photograph or on the last photograph, the two buses, they mean nothing to me. It means nothing to me if two buses are parked somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a tank in the film a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw different artillery weapons, artillery pieces, on the film previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the road, on an asphalt road, and it was operating. But when we came by it wasn't there, because we wouldn't have been able to pass the buses and trucks, and that's why I say that they weren't there at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: In the film I played just a moment ago, there was a tank in the film. Did you see that image of the tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was it a tank or was it an APC?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll find the specific spot; I'm going to show you the tank in just a minute. But did you see any tanks at all along the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all, not a single one, or any other artillery pieces. Only infantry weapons. And that could have lasted -- the whole trip could have lasted about an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you went through Nova Kasaba, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Nova Kasaba, Milici, Vlasenica, that is, the communication line towards Han Pijesak and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 12/2 placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I only have a few minutes, Mr. President. I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to divide up our time. I should like to ask you when you're -- when you think you're going to finish. It is now twenty minutes past twelve.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I should finish within 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more. Because I thought that we could go up to half past twelve, but we'll give you until 12.35.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a picture of -- an aerial image, taken at approximately 2.00 on the 13th of July, of a football field by which the main road passes, and in this picture there are identified a large group of prisoners who are being detained on the football field. In addition to that, Witness D/C, we have had a number of witnesses, including a Dutch witness named Captain Egbers, who testified he was at this location and he saw a number of prisoners, hundreds of prisoners, on this football field. When you passed on the 13th of July through Nova Kasaba, did you see any Muslim prisoners being detained by VRS soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see the field either, the football field. I didn't pay attention. Had there been people there, I'm sure I would have noticed. But I didn't notice the football field at all. This was at 1400 hours. I passed by in the morning hours, so I can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your testimony that at no time on route from Bratunac to Zepa did you see a single Muslim prisoner being detained by the VRS soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, not from a car. No, I couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 771, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman by the name of Colonel Popovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see Colonel Popovic next to General Krstic in this image?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He has a moustache. It could be him, possibly it is, but it needn't be. It looks like him, but I wouldn't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Colonel Popovic in Srebrenica on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really say. I saw him somewhere, I did see him somewhere, whether it was Srebrenica or Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on a little bit in your testimony and ask you -- you testified on direct examination about who you saw in Zepa, and in response to my colleague's question, you said you saw both General Krstic, General Mladic, and the Main Staff officers, including General Tolimir, Beara, and others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see them in Zepa? Where was it that you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them at the forward command post of Krivaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately when did you see Colonel Beara at the forward command post in Krivaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of the operation, that was for sure. But I saw him several times. I think Beara or Tolimir, that they were negotiating with the Muslims. I didn't know them very well but I just saw them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Colonel Beara with General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Krstic, I saw him more because he would tour the units. He visited the soldiers, the units, the command. I don't think he was there when I saw them all gathered there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Colonel Popovic down at the forward command post in Krivaca? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him somewhere. Whether it was at Srebrenica or it was Zepa, I don't know. He was present, but it's difficult for me now. I can't quite remember where I actually saw him, but I did see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you ever see General Zivanovic down at Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did at the beginning of the operation, that he was there. But he wasn't there later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was wrong with General Zivanovic's physical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that anything was wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did he leave the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many have asked themselves that question. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would have been the answers to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't answer that here. There is some information which is not for this Court; they are rumours, hearsay. But I didn't know that he was ill because he looked quite all right physically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the rumours and the hearsay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then I'll say what it was. One of the rumours, later on, on the streets when you socialised with people, with the ordinary people, you could hear that General Zivanovic was replaced because of the massacre at Srebrenica, and that all this was laid at the door of General Krstic. But those are only rumours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you attend any going-away party or any handover-of-duties ceremony between General Zivanovic and General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not -- I was not present, but my Commander, Mirko Trivic, he -- there was a restaurant between Sokolac and Han Pijesak. I think the name of it was Jela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that there was a handover ceremony where General Mladic went to Vlasenica on the morning of the 13th of July, he assembled the staff of the Vlasenica Drina Corps headquarters, and he announced to the soldiers and staff at the Vlasenica headquarters that General Krstic was now the Commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. My Commander, Colonel Mirko Trivic, received an invitation to attend the seeing-off ceremony of General Zivanovic who was retiring, and that was at that restaurant. It was in the middle of combat operations so we weren't quite clear -- we didn't have time to pay attention to that at all. And the knowledge that the next Commander was Krstic, it was about seven -- we learnt about that seven days after we arrived at Zepa that he had been -- we were informed about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I have only a few questions left. Did the VRS massacre hundreds of unarmed Muslim civilians and prisoners of war following the takeover of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question because I don't know. All I know about that is via the media, the information media. If that really did happen, which I find -- nobody can believe, then that is really a crime. But I state once again that General Krstic would never have ordered anything like that and that he did not know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my question is: (redacted) (redacted). It's been five years since the massacres took place. They have been verified --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- by international observers. There have been a series of exhumations that have revealed the bodies of hundreds of prisoners with their hands tied, with their heads blindfolded. Now, that information has been available for a number of years, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that the VRS massacred those civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I saw all that documentation, but all of it has been reproduced by the Federation, the Muslim Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot believe it. I find it difficult to believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you just some last questions. When was the first time that you heard about these massacres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite a long time later. I thought it was -- I think it was the autumn of that year, when it began to be rumoured. Before that nobody knew about it, the population, the army, the people. And I learnt about that through the information media because up till then they were closed off. We didn't know much. When General Krstic was arrested, then we received different information about everything and evidence and pictures, photographs, although, as a human being I can't conceive of it being at all possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, shortly after the massacres -- after the fall of Srebrenica took place, and many of these massacres took place in public areas in the Zvornik municipality - one major massacre took place at the Kravica warehouse, the warehouse by which you passed on the morning of the 13th - those massacres which were quite public in nature were known to the civilian population and known to the military that participated in those. You've been a soldier, remain a soldier. Is it your testimony that after these massacres took place you didn't hear any information about the massacres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not immediately after. Perhaps two to three months went by when something like that was talked about, but not at all those figures. And there was no official information in the command or via the information that it had actually taken place. It was only in 1990-something. When General Krstic was arrested, well, then, the story began to be recounted and that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you personally acquired information about those massacres, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not personally, no. There was no official information ever from the Superior Command. But it was for the most part from the information media, and the Muslim information media at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do to attempt to verify, since you were involved in morale and you needed to inform the subordinate soldiers who were in your units whether these rumours were correct, what did you do to attempt to verify this information that was quite common?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We learnt that after peace was established, when the unit was demobilised. The postal code has young conscripts now. But all those rumours and all those events around Srebrenica could not be verified, nor could any information be obtained, nor was it possible to have any influence over that. Even people in much higher positions, not to mention ordinary officers and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, wouldn't those allegations, if true, directly affect the morale of the soldiers in the VRS? And wasn't it your responsibility to ensure that the morale of the soldiers was maintained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To maintain the morale, yes. But these allegations were made by the Muslim side. Information obtained from the media cannot be disseminated be they Serbian or Muslim media, because during the war and after the war, there were so many discrepancies, there were many untruths. There were various political parties, each one with their own version. And our responsibility is to reproduce information that we receive down the chain of command. But we never received any such information in that manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And information that you also received and disseminated was information about United Nations' Resolutions related to Srebrenica, and there were United Nations' Resolutions that dealt with the missing of Srebrenica. Was that a source that was questionable in your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Officially we did not receive that Resolution in the unit; we just heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, another question. It's already two minutes beyond your time. So this is your last question. Be careful choosing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've thought about it already. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it, Witness D/C, that you learned that the Supreme Commander, Radovan Karadzic, and the head of the army, Ratko Mladic, were indicted for the events in Srebrenica by the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot remember the date. But we did learn about it. I think this was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you just gave us an exhibit 757 with a picture. Is it relevant to any of your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is not. We will make an offer -- we will tender certain of those exhibits into evidence. That will not be one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon, especially for your cooperation. We are now going to have the long break. But before that, I should like you, Mr. Harmon, to communicate to the Defence the extracts that you used so that we will try and divide up the time so as to give a little time to the Defence to prepare. But as we're having the big break now, I think that the Defence will be able to review those extracts before the re-examination. So we are intentionally having the break now so that the Defence will have time to review those texts for its re-examination. So we are now going to have an hour-long break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I just clarify one thing on this, because I'm not sure I understood myself. As far as what you have to give the Defence, I understand it's just -- is it just, what you're going to give them, the extract which you've already quoted into the record, or is it any other material that deals with that precise subject matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I had intended to give them just the extracts, but I can give them just a little bit more to deal with the subject matter itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I would feel more comfortable then. I know it isn't going to be true, but we always have the hypothetical that in the next line, somebody gives a sentence that, you know, goes against what came before. So I think that would make everybody, certainly me, feel more comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will do that. No problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. A one-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Witness D/C, you are going to answer questions now put to you by Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Petrusic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence will not re-examine this witness for long. We shall take advantage of the material disclosed to us by the Prosecution in the break to put questions regarding it. Re-examined by Mr. Petrusic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, in a statement given by your Commander, Colonel Trivic, to the Office of the Prosecutor in Banja Luka on the 5th of October, page 39, it says, among other things, that on the 12th of July, between 10.00 and 11.00 a.m., officers received orders at the Bojna repeater, that they gathered there and that they received certain instructions and orders. Then he goes on to say in his statement that present there were Colonel Andric, Colonel Vicic, and General Krstic; also, that Colonel Vicic was the one who chaired the meeting and that Krstic was present. So the time we are talking about is the 12th of July, between 10.00 and 11.00. In the course of these proceedings, we have established without dispute, I would say, and we have witness statements to that effect and a videotape, that on the 12th of July, between 10.00 and 12.00, General Krstic was present at a meeting in the Fontana Hotel with representatives of the Dutch Battalion, representatives of the Muslim population, and other VRS officers were present. So reviewing the statement of your Commander, Colonel Trivic, it appears that General Krstic was simultaneously at two different places, at Bojna and at the Fontana Hotel. Have you any comment to make regarding this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Bojna, on that date, on the 12th, I did not see General Krstic, or at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also showed -- quoted from a statement in which your Commander claims that on the 13th of July he took a different route to go to Zepa rather than the route via Srebrenica-Potocari-Bratunac-Konjevic Polje to go to Zepa, the route that you have described. Are you now sure that you and Colonel Trivic and your signalsman together took the route that you told us about in your examination-in-chief, and also during the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm quite certain of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness D/C, we heard from you today for the first time, and that is the first time I hear of it too, that in the area of Zepa, for a certain time, Colonel Beara was also present. Do you know what he was doing there? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was present. I think he was involved in the negotiations, and he was also Chief of Security. He and General Tolimir conducted the negotiations. I don't know exactly what they talked about, but we got certain information about offensive operations and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you know that he and General Tolimir were engaged in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those negotiations were between who and who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between the Serb side, the army of Republika Srpska, and the Muslim side, actually representatives of Zepa municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Beara and General Tolimir are officers of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, are they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. President. My friend Visnjic is drawing my attention to the transcript regarding the interruption of offensive operations. So let me repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you received orders to halt offensive operations because of the negotiations at Boksanica Mountain with the Muslim side and other representatives; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness D/C. I can't say your name. I just want to have a clearer perception of what you went through since you almost graduated -- you said you graduated as a professor. Were you ever a professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I never worked as a professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you had the title. You said that in the beginning of your testimony, that you had the title of professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you preferred to be an officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted). Now, what was your role, exactly, when you said that at the beginning, in 1990, you were really interested in raising the morale and giving the soldiers the perception of taking part in a war and solidarity? What was, exactly, this mission? Against whom was this war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted), an unexpected situation occurred for the former Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the Serbian people in the republic. A war broke out, conflicts which later developed into an all-out war and conflicts and hostilities. The role for the organ for Information, Moral Guidance, and Religious Affairs was to explain to the soldiers the truth and to provide them the indicators as to what situation we were in, why we were in that situation, how to deal with crisis situations that they may encounter in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean, as a catalyst to direct them against what you call the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Our lines were defensive lines, and the Serb army was not always attacking, it was mostly defending and protecting the Serb civilian population from the attacks by Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. As far as attacks are concerned, I will go now to 1995, in Srebrenica. You mentioned today that there was no resistance from Muslim forces on July 10th and you took control very easily of the area, and therefore they did not have to shoot much. So there was no attack in that part in that time, in that area of Srebrenica? Did I understand you rightly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you did. One can't say there were no attacks, but there were no operations of any greater intensity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But Srebrenica, in that case, was not really shelled, the city itself, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that very well. It was not shelled at all. Not a single shell fell on the urban area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But when you went in, there was nobody in it, was there? It was a deserted city, except for this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- Serb whom you saw killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw two Muslims, and the third, a woman, was a Serb. The people had abandoned the town and headed towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The whole population fled, ran away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We entered a completely deserted Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted), why did they run away? Why was it a deserted village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that when the Serb army reached their initial positions, they themselves requested to go to the territory of the Federation, because as far as I know, they could have stayed behind. They could have surrendered and stayed on, but they all said that they wanted to leave because they didn't want to live in a location where Serb authority had been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'll not dwell on that. It was very -- I was very interested in listening to you telling us about how General Krstic was loved by his soldiers, and this is something very understandable. He cared for them. You also told us that he visited them in hospitals and so on. Was he, in other words, also -- you know when you love someone very much, you can let him do what he likes. So was he permissive? Would he allow them certain eccentricities, violations, and not really hold them accountable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In the unit there was strict discipline, and precisely because of that discipline the troops and officers respected him. It was an organised entity where everything functioned normally. And whenever he addressed soldiers or officers, he always drew their attention to their behaviour, how they should behave, how they should conduct the war. He was a soldier, a real soldier, and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So for the sake of popularity, he would not sacrifice discipline and accountability.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Though he was so strict and introduced strict discipline, he was loved and respected, because he was also a just man, a fair man. In all the situations we found ourselves in, he always had the right solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, being strict, do you have any instance where he applied this discipline by punishing soldiers or holding them accountable for violations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases. Many soldiers at the beginning of 1992 and many people who were mobilised to our units were refugees from Zenica, Sarajevo, and various other places, so they were extremely indignant about everything that had happened to them. They had lost their homes; some of them, family members. They joined the unit and they tried to behave in the way they wanted. For instance, if a Muslim was captured, there were cases that they wanted to kill him, not just to kill him but to somehow take their revenge on him for what they had been through, but he was always against that. And this was something that was so pronounced. He attached the greatest importance to this, saying that prisoners of war must not be hurt, be he a soldier or a civilian, a man or a woman. He was against torching of buildings, against destruction. He was a rare officer who behaved fully in accordance with international conventions, the respect of human rights, and a correct attitude in spite of everything a war entails.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You being in the Information Department, do you have any specific cases where he really did practice that and he had authority to do it, or was it just as a principle which was not put into action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. It was always put into action, it was put into practice, and that's why we're so fully aware of it. I mentioned that we had Muslim prisoners who were kept for more than a year near the brigade headquarters, and I said how he treated them. As in any army, there were extremists, uneducated, illiterate people who had lost their homes and families, who wanted to make up for it in a way by killing that person or mistreating them. But, no, no one dared do any such thing because of him, and that is how it was always. And now suddenly nobody understands why General Krstic should be accused for Srebrenica and accused for the death of such an enormous number of people, which we can hardly conceive of being killed. We just don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did he have the authority to punish, or just to give orders to the soldiers not to commit anything? But did he have real authority to punish anybody who really committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While he was the Brigade Commander, he had the authority of a Brigade Commander, and the Commander has the greatest powers. He could punish, he could give orders. Later when he became Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, he no longer had such powers because, as in all the other armies in the world, it is well known who is authorised to issue orders. A Chief of Staff does not have the competence to issue orders but to organise operations, combat, together with the Operations Department. But I think that he has no right to issue orders except if so authorised by the Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You, in fact, mentioned that - I just found it in my notes - he was very kind to the prisoners and he sometimes exchanged them. Did he have authority to exchange the prisoners? Was it within the authority of a Commander, or was it a political thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time when he was the Commander, he had the authority to exchange, but he also -- for some prisoners to be exchanged, certain bodies had to exist to actually carry out the exchange. He could just propose that he would give so many people for exchange, but there were services and bodies who actually engaged in those exchanges. I think it was the Security Organs and the civilian MUPs or the police; I think they were responsible for all these exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But what was his role, then? Did he suggest -- was he a promoter of exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he would make a suggestion. For instance, he would say, "I have war prisoners in the unit," and then he would make a request for them to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And his requests were usually obeyed and thought highly of as a General? What was his prestige?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While he was Commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, he had the rank of Colonel, so his authority regarding the area of responsibility of his brigade and the municipality covered by that brigade was extremely high. He was respected as officers used to be in the former Yugoslavia. And later when he became a General, he still enjoyed high prestige and a great deal of respect. But as for the respect of his superiors, I cannot say much about that because I am not familiar with those relationships.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, but you are an information officer. You are the person who sees everything. So his status in the army was a high one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that he took, in fact, very strong positions. He did it with the Croats, apparently, and he saved -- he saved Croats. I won't go into the details again. Was that taken against him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said many people, ordinary people, and even some of the troops were against this, because this was already in 1993 when the combat was very intensive, and this did not affect a small group but an entire municipality inhabited by Croats, their soldiers, and equipment. And he helped them, both the civilians and the military, to go to Sokolac, and from there on, where they wanted. And I remember there were people saying, "Who does he think he is to be able to transfer Croatian soldiers?" It wasn't really something that they applauded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He did that to save them from the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did he do something on the other side, to save Muslims from Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He saved some Muslims. The village of Crna Rijeka, at the Nisic plateau, a little later they too came to Sokolac. So I remember that they were accommodated right next to the Croats. There were no other facilities that were close by. So minor arguments, disputes, occurred between them but a stop was put to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And in this instance, also, was he looked upon as having acted in some kind of unorthodox way, in a way that was not so nationalistic? Was he reproached by his superiors? I'm not talking about his inferiors but the great authorities. Do you know if he was blamed or discarded or anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially he was not charged; I don't believe he was discarded either. Only by public opinion, the general public, and some soldiers who disapproved, until he explained why this was necessary, and then he calmed them down. But we were always involved in combat. There was a war going on, things were happening, so there wasn't much time always to think about things in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, but there would be a policy, a line of policy, perhaps, to bring up someone and to bring down someone. So General Krstic belonged to which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was put down precisely as a result of politics. He didn't deserve it. He should have continued advancing in his career and he should have been the main commander of the Serb army. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Don't you think the fact that he replaced Zivanovic at an early age was a sign of appreciation? And President Karadzic praised him as a great officer, in spite of you saying that he had this precedent of being kind to both Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they expressed their appreciation only on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just in passing, my last question: You just mentioned Beara. You said he was present at Zepa and he conducted negotiations. What was his relationship with General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think they had a good relationship. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness D/C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald, if you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness D/C, I have only two questions. Do you remember the date or approximately the time that Beara was in Zepa? I know you were there sometime from the 13th of July to the 2nd of August, I think. Can you place the time that he was there within that framework?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within that framework, the 13th/14th, I didn't see him. But I think on the 15th onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you saw him several times from the 15th on, when he was involved in negotiations --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. My second question is this: Given that what you told us was part of the prime parts of your job, which was to reassure the soldiers about what was going on in the outside world and what they might hear other places, during the time from, say, July 12th or 13th all the way through to August 2nd, which is the date you say you left Zepa, did you hear from -- no matter how much you discredit it, but did you actually hear over the radio or the TV or by rumours that may have come from the Muslim sources, but nonetheless, did you actually hear anything about the complaints about the disappearance of some of the survivors of Srebrenica? No matter how much you didn't think it was true or you couldn't believe it, did you actually hear any of those rumours or accusations during that whole period? On the radio. We have had other witnesses who have told us that they heard, within the week after July 12th or 13th, from Muslim sources, over the radio, accusations about disappearances. Did you hear any of those? Even if you didn't believe them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not hear them. My units had its active combat operations underway, and Zepa, they call it the municipality of Zepa, but it's an enormous area with no electricity. We didn't actually have the means by which to hear about it, and we didn't have time to listen to anything like that. Events followed each other in rapid succession. We had to move all the time, so that nobody talked about that. We didn't discuss anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Is that true all the way through to August 2nd -- by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. August 2nd Zepa had already been captured or liberated. But still, even after the active combat was over, you still didn't hear anything, and none of the soldiers came to you and said that they had heard it or that sort of thing? Not until after you left Zepa did you get any idea; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Yes, that's right. We heard something later on, much later on, but we didn't pay attention. Nobody mentioned any figures of that kind for the victims. And even when people started talking about it, we didn't believe it, and that's how the years passed. And now it would appear that it actually did take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald. Witness D/C, I have a few questions for you as well. You said that the Information Service (redacted) had as its objective to furnish a realistic image of the situation. Now, what do you mean by "realistic, a realistic image"? What does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish to say that it was our task to show the realistic state of affairs in the encirclement -- immediate encirclement and further off in the unit, in the state, in the country, outside the borders of the former Yugoslavia. But they were information which we -- the information we reproduced was the information that we received from the Corps command, which was our Superior Command. And even if we heard something by the way or learned something by the way, we were not allowed and were not able to convey that to the soldiers. It was only official information that we received from our Superior Commands that we had the right to pass on to the men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What, therefore, in order to construct that reality, was the place or the role of radiowaves and the mass media that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the role of the mass media on public opinion was not considered too much because different stations put out different information, and different television stations would present the same event in a different way. So that that information was not reliable information. Of course, the soldiers could listen to all the different media. But as morally ourselves, that's what we called ourselves, we had to indicate and guide them towards seeing what was true and what was false, and in order to do this, we received instructions from our Superior Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your service, did it diffuse information to the media as well? Did you supply the media with information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were able to inform the media about the situation in our unit, how far we were moving, how we were holding our positions. We did have cooperation with local information media, and for this information to be channelled towards state television, this was done, once again, through the Superior Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say that information via the media were not trustworthy, how were you able to trust whether they were trustworthy or not? How were you able to arrive at that conclusion as to trustworthiness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that the criteria was set by the Superior Command. We ourselves were not able to do this. We had different information. So if an event took place outside the zone of our unit, we were not able to do this on the basis of what the media said, and not only the Serbian media, because they too -- information was different there too. Then we had the Croat media and the Muslim media. So we did know that something was going on but we couldn't really distinguish what. And then the Department for Moral Guidance, Information, and Religious Affairs would get instructions from the Superior Command and pass it on down the line to the subordinate levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this process of constructing reality, building up a picture of reality, did you try to take in information from, may I say, the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was information via the media from the enemy side, so the Intelligence Organs and Security Organs were in charge of collecting all this information. The work of my own department was in that -- for example, if the enemy side exerted psychological propaganda towards a unit, then we should try and prevent that kind of propaganda if it was false, and for the most part it was false. So that was our task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, did you intercept communication between two parties on the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What type of interception did you engage in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me now to explain what these devices were called, but we did have devices through which we were able to monitor and intercept the conversations and decode them. And if there was information that the enemy was preparing for attack, then we would pass the information on. If there were pieces of information that were less important, then we didn't send them further on down the line. They were just set aside, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people who did these interceptions, were they really preoccupied with informing -- reporting on what they actually heard, on what they really heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was the -- the people who worked on these devices, these people were trained in the area of communications and that was their sole assignment. That's all they -- that's the only thing they knew how to do. Later on it was the Intelligence Organs, Security Organs, who would pass down any relevant information to us and so on, that went down to the units afterwards, after it had been sifted through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, Witness D/C, imagine the following situation, if you will: You are given a report by somebody and he says, "I've written down what I heard when I intercepted a communication," for example, with regard to a combat, a battle of some kind. What would you do with that report? Would it be a credible, reliable, trustworthy report, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not always. It depended on who the person who had intercepted it was and who had heard it, because there were -- people wanted to plant different pieces of information; for example, the enemy would like to plant information and lead us astray. So it would depend on the person working in this communication system and how far he was able to detect this, because there were efforts to mislead us. So there were cases even on our side where -- so it's not always trustworthy, no. You can have a change of voice. It is not always reliable and absolutely trustworthy information, but sometimes it can be of assistance, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another question: You spoke about the enormous number of deaths when you spoke about the Srebrenica events, the enormous figures that were mentioned. Now, after the 2nd of August, when did you hear for the first time about these events? When was the first time you heard of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I returned from Zepa, I did not hear anything about that because my unit was still engaged in combat activity and holding defensive lines, and the lines were attacked by the Muslims of Olovo and Kladanj. So we were engaged in that defence. So it was October/November when there were certain intimations that something had happened. But as I say, it was only when General Krstic was arrested that we actually learnt of it via the information media, and in different ways we began to hear more and more about all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, the zone between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac, that area, is it as populated with respect to -- what was the situation like there? Were there a lot of people living in that area, in Bratunac, for example? Was it a highly-populated area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, in Bratunac, the town did have a large population. I went to Srebrenica and Bratunac then for the first time. During the Srebrenica operation, I passed through Bratunac. That's the first time I'd been there. We passed through that village, and there is a Serbian village called Kravica, and it had a lot of inhabitants. I think in 1993 it was completely destroyed and burnt to the ground, and I saw these houses that were destroyed and burnt down to the ground beside the roadway, the roadside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So after having learnt about everything that had taken place, that there were hundreds of people who had been killed, who had been transported in cars, who had been interned, and so on, was it possible that all that had taken place without the public knowing, without the people knowing? The general public. I'm not speaking about military men, just the people, the public. Could the people have known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably. But why that was not expressed through the public information media. It didn't exist on the Serb media; a little perhaps in the Muslim media. That was the situation right up until two years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the general public, if people generally could have known, then people with military authority, could they have known as well or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, probably some of them did know. But the majority of them did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you knew General Krstic well. Do you know whether General Krstic may have shared knowledge of the existence, or at least the probability of the rumours regarding those events? Was General Krstic in a position to know? No, let me make myself clear. Did you know whether he knew? Did you know whether he knew, in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was he in a position to know to the same extent that the general public knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not in a position to know because, from the 13th on, he was rarely at Zepa. Fighting was going on. He must have learnt something at some point later on. He was in the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you said that he may have known something later, can you tell us when? When you say "later," could you tell us when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not thinking of a long period of time, but I assume at some point, I assume that somebody must have said what had been going on, because I saw that General Krstic - I don't know how to put it - he was a terribly bitter man. Later on, when he was Corps Commander, I had the impression that he was having problems of some sort, because as the Chief of Staff and as the Corps Commander, after Srebrenica, when the headquarters was in Vlasenica, he would often come to the base of our unit because it was his original unit, and he would often visit the troops. So we had contacts with him. We didn't talk about Srebrenica much. But he was in a rather strange mood. And now that I think back, I think that he felt awfully sorry that this had happened and that he was unable to do anything about it. That is my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are telling us that General Krstic became rather bitter. Could you explain to us more or less when this was? You mentioned his becoming Commander of the Drina Corps. I am not sure that I understood you correctly regarding the timing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not when he became Commander, but much later in 1995, when the active combat ended throughout Republika Srpska. There was some more fighting in Bosnia and Krajina. But I had a feeling that something was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. You have finished your testimony here in the Tribunal. Thank you very much for coming. I wish to congratulate you once again on your birthday, and I wish you a safe journey to your place of residence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I wish to thank this Honourable Tribunal for their hospitality and for their cordiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you need to wait a few more minutes because the usher is not here to escort you out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Petrusic, I see that Mr. Harmon is about to get up. Yes, Mr. Harmon, I think that we have some exhibits to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tendered two exhibits in the course of this examination; one is Prosecutor's Exhibit 791, which is a Bratunac Brigade casualty report, and one is a new video compilation, Prosecutor's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Exhibit 766. Now, in respect of Prosecutor's Exhibit 766, there were five subparts to that exhibit. I showed Witness D/C three of those subparts. We therefore seek admission to the subparts of Prosecutors Exhibit 766, subparts 3, 4, and 5. I might add, for the record, that the two subparts that were not offered have been taken from a previous exhibit that was offered as part of the Petrovic film that we have introduced previously. But for purposes of this 766, we are only offering subparts 3, 4, and 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has no objection regarding Exhibit 766, subparts 3, 4, and 5. However, regarding Exhibit 791, it was tendered during the testimony of Witness D/C. This is a report about members of the Bratunac Brigade, and I am trying to discover the reason for tendering this document now because this witness did not speak about individual members of various entities. She identified them on the road from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje as members of the army and the police but not specifically. We can neither contest this list because we are aware of the source. This is just my comment regarding this exhibit. And as for the trustworthiness of this exhibit, the Defence has no doubts at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, what is the usefulness and its link with this testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This exhibit is offered, Your Honours, for the reason that this witness testified that on the 13th of July she observed army soldiers and police along the road of Bratunac-Milici Brigade engaged in combat with Muslim units. The Defence yesterday offered Exhibit D25, which is a map that shows the location of various Bratunac Brigade units that were involved in the sweeping operation. It is alongside the Bratunac-Milici Brigade; it is in the Bratunac area of responsibility. And we tender the Exhibit 791 only for purposes of showing that there were no casualties. And if there was, in fact, active combat along that particular road, one would have expected in this casualty report to have seen some deaths and the like. It's our view that this evidence, 791, is an exhibit which demonstrates circumstantially that if there was combat -- it demonstrates directly that if there was combat, there were no casualties suffered by the Bratunac Brigade members, and one can infer -- and its relevance is that one can infer that if there was combat in this period of time along this road, it wasn't very active. But whatever inference can be drawn from the exhibit can be made by the Trial Chamber. We will argue the relevance of the exhibit during our summation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may. It is, of course, up to you to decide, but I feel that reference by Mr. Harmon to the map drawn for us yesterday should not be linked to this exhibit, the deployment of units of the Bratunac Brigade on the 14th of July, following orders of the Commander of that brigade, Vidoje Blagojevic. So we have spoken about that at length. Therefore, the testimony of this witness relates to the 13th of July, and the deployment referred to by my learned friend occurred a day later. So that the Defence still maintains its position. But this is just my remark regardless of the use that this document may be put to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber rules to admit the two exhibits, 791, and the Chamber will attach probative value as it sees fit to this document; and Exhibit 766/3, /4, and /5 are also admitted. We now have 20 minutes. Do you have a witness, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, we have two more witnesses for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two for today? But can one stay for tomorrow or do we have to hear them today? If not, we'll divide them up so we have ten minutes for each.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our plan and our schedule, we had expected that Witness D/C's testimony would take much shorter; however, the Prosecutor has obviously many questions to ask, so we have planned two more witnesses. One is in reserve. We have another 20 minutes, so it is up to Your Honours to decide whether we should begin with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's do that. Yes, let's begin with the witness to make the best of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness has not asked for any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I please have the name of the next witness for the court reporters?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Vlado Rudovic is the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. President and Your Honours, I have provided to the Defence certain pages of a transcript of an interview with Colonel Trivic, and I would request that those pages now be returned to us and not be disseminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was merely for you to prepare for the re-examination. As far as I know, the Defence has the statement of this witness, so does the Prosecution, as far as I've been able to understand. Yes, we're waiting for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can. Good afternoon. I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to give you, please, Mr. Rudovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Please make yourself as comfortable as you can. Are you feeling relaxed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much for coming, Mr. Rudovic. You are going to answer questions which the Defence attorney, Mr. Petrusic, who is standing to your left, is going to put to you, and after that there will be questions from the Prosecutor and the Judges. But now it is Mr. Petrusic. You have the floor, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Petrusic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudovic, before we start, I know that you're a little nervous, and it is quite natural that you should be, but as the President of the Chamber has already suggested, please relax. At any time you can have a drink of water. And you will see that this is a perfectly normal situation and we will get through it easily. So, Mr. Rudovic, will you please tell us when and where you were born, where you lived, where you're living now; very briefly, your particulars, personal particulars?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Do I need to give the date? The 23rd of September, 1934, in Sokolac, that is where I was born. And I've been living in Han Pijesak since 1952.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I assume you're a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a pensioner living in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudovic, tell us, since when were you a participant in the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean this war? This war? That other one or this one, this last one? Because I was in both wars, the Second World War and this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since you've touched upon the subject, tell us, you participated in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a boy then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I assume you were a courier.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was young and I was a courier, and I did other such simple tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
