utterances.text: What about your participation in this war that started in 1992 and went on to 1995?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: I was a participant from the 13th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can it be said that you were mobilised on the 13th of August?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were quite well-advanced in age.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was getting along, but I wanted to be a volunteer. I was forced to be a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the reasons that prompted you to volunteer to the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 7th of August, 1992, they killed my son, the Muslims, who now call themselves Bosniaks, and this prompted me to take up arms and to go to war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your son was killed in action?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: He was killed in the village. Six of them were killed there; a woman of 75 or 76, another man of 75 or 76, another one of 70, and they slit the throat of a total invalid, a young man, and then they killed this teacher and my son. This was no combat, it was murder. After my son's funeral, I joined the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say that you volunteered, I assume you reported to a military district or the Territorial Defence or whatever it was that was taking in people?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a military district for the able-bodied men, and I volunteered. They registered me. I personally asked for that unit; they didn't assign me to any unit. I asked to join.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which unit was it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: The position where my son used to be in my place, in my village, Borovine. There is film on that, the killings, the torching. And I joined there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you joined at the beginning of August, that is, the 8th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: No, the 13th of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The 13th of August, 1992. Tell us briefly, were there any combat operations there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: There were then and not afterwards for a couple of days, because they captured some people at Veliki Zep, those young soldiers. Then there was negotiations, blackmail; I don't know exactly how much, but about 50 or 60 tonnes of flour, fuel, NAFTA salt, I don't know what, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rudovic, please speak more slowly, because of the interpreters, when answering my questions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So let us make things clear. This is the region of Han Pijesak, where you were.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the area of the municipality of Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in those villages around Han Pijesak, on one side was Serb villages and on the other, Muslim villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That is the line that separates them, because these were not mixed villages as in many other places. They were purely Muslim villages, and over here to the right, Serb villages. Not just the one village, but all villages along an area of 20 kilometres. Why that was so, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there armed conflicts at that time between the Muslim army and you, that is, the Serb army, along that line of separation between those villages?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: No, not until they attacked that village. There were no operations. But then, after they attacked, the operations started. And these kept attacking, these others defending, and that is how it was. And then the Romanija Brigade came and formed a line; the leadership of the 2nd Romanija formed a line. They pushed them back. This line was in between the villages, you see, so they couldn't approach us, nor could we approach them. There was a distance of some 4 or 5 kilometres between us and the line and between them and the line; the line was in between, in other words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So along that line, was there any movement? Were there any combat operations? Was anything happening?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. There weren't many troops there. They could pass where they wanted. They went into villages behind our backs; they stole livestock; they killed elderly people who were all unfit for combat, they stayed home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us be quite clear about this. So the period you are talking about is the period prior to the formation of the safe area.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1992. Only 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When preparing for your testimony, you told me that there was a group of soldiers there who were killed in 1992, at the beginning of 1992. Just a moment, please. Let me finish my question. Then you make a pause of 10 or 20 seconds, and only then give your answer. Please bear this in mind because of the interpreters. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: This was on the 4th of June. They went to the repeater, Zlovrh; there was a military repeater there. There were some 15 soldiers there. Vehicles were carrying fuel and food and I don't know what. They passed through three villages. Nobody did anything to them, nor did they hurt anyone, and when they reached that spot, they were killed. I took part in pulling out the dead. It was a terrible sight; a normal man couldn't describe it. They were burnt. Casings were pushed into their eyes and set on fire. I found a woman, a nurse, of 22 or 23, totally naked, cut across this way and that way, lying dead in the meadow. And when we pulled out the dead from there, the line fell, and this went on like that until they attacked Borovine. When they attacked Borovine, the line moved 4 or 5 kilometres, this line between the villages. And they kept on with their provocation but we didn't return fire much. Somebody was giving us orders and they told us not to fire back. It was in October when we went back to the villages, and then during the winter they started their provocations again and we had to withdraw again. So sometime in April the situation was placed under control. Lieutenant Colonel Krstic was in charge of the operation. He ordered us to halt and he explained to us what a safe area meant - this was already in May - that we mustn't shoot, that we mustn't go there, that they were disarmed, that we had to observe this. So very few of us were left behind, and so we joined the protective regiment which was left there simply to keep order. But they did not respect this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us go back for a moment to 1992. On the 13th of August, you became a member of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, and you said that in April or May, the Lieutenant Colonel explained to you what a safe area meant. Was this April 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 1993, because we withdrew in October 1992, and in spring 1993 we went back to our old positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Lieutenant Colonel Krstic, now General Krstic, his first name is Radislav --

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- did you meet him for the first time then?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I saw him from before because his wife is from Han Pijesak. He was an officer; he served somewhere. But this was the first time I was with him personally, just then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1993. About the end of April, beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time he was Commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us in more detail whether you personally saw him?

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: When all this was explained to us and what our role should be, that they had been disarmed down there and that we mustn't do anything, that we had to take care, that people could till their land normally, that even Muslims would be allowed to go on tilling their land and that we mustn't hurt them, then I asked him, "Mr. Krstic, do you know that my son's son and my own son were killed? They were not killed, they were murdered." And I said, "You see what it looks like. He kills my son and I mustn't do anything. If he kills my son, I'll kill him too." And he says, "No, you mustn't." He was an officer but I am older. But then he said, "Look, it's a safe area and it must not be done. Is that clear?" I said, "Clear." How can it be clear to me that I can't go there and he can? He can. I'm talking about Krstic, Mr. Krstic. We had quite an argument there. He said to me, "You must not. I don't want to be a war criminal because of the likes of you." And there was a young soldier next to me, and he said, "You mustn't take an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth," and he turned around and left. I didn't see Krstic again, and I really can't tell you when it was again -- maybe 1994. Then he was wounded, and after that I didn't see him again until 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you had that argument with Krstic and when you expressed your fury, Krstic said that he would not be a criminal because of the likes of you.

utterances.speaker: VLADO RUDOVIC
utterances.text: He said a Serb soldier must be a normal person, he must act normally. "I told you already that no one may attack civilians, but only if they attack you." So I have to wait to be attacked. If I see him armed, I can capture him. "Once you capture him, you can't do this or that to him. You have to hand him over." So there were no problems. They did make incursions, though. There was about 7 kilometres between two positions, and they would pass through there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we will have to stop there and we will continue tomorrow, of course, with the Chamber's permission and because of the working hours which have run out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I take advantage of this opportunity. If we could listen to the tape again. Page 99, rows 5 through 13, could corrections be made, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I think the interpreters have some difficulties. Could you repeat what you just said? What was your request? What was your remark?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My remark relates to the translation at page 99, between rows 5 and 13. I'd rather not go into the details now, but I suggest that the interpreters listen to the tape again and correct the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be more practical - I think the interpreters agree with this procedure - that it is much better for you to put the question and for us to hear the answer again. Do you agree that we go on for a couple of more minutes? I think there's something that wasn't quite correctly interpreted. So maybe you could repeat the question and we can wait and hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to take advantage of this afternoon, Mr. President, to look through the transcript, and then I will put my question to the witness again tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a good suggestion, yes. You're going to read the transcript and put the question again to the witness. In any event, I thank the interpreters for their willingness to stay on a little longer. So, Mr. Rudovic, we will stop there now and we will have the pleasure of seeing you again tomorrow at 9.20. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of November, 2000, at 9.20 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
